question.text: Mr. Ramesh Iyer, CIO of Aravalli Long-Short Fund (a Cat III open-ended AIF), is explaining onboarding material to a prospective HNI family office. The family currently parks INR 40 crore in 91-day T-bills 'as savings' and another INR 60 crore in the fund unit class. Which statement BEST captures the saving-versus-investment distinction as articulated in the NISM chapter?

answer.text: Savings and investment are interchangeable because both involve setting aside money earned over money spent.

Saving is simply income minus expenditure typically parked in highly-liquid short-term instruments, while investment is a current commitment of that saving to specific asset classes with a longer horizon expecting a higher return.
Every saver is automatically an investor the moment the money enters a bank deposit, irrespective of time horizon.
Investment is defined as any capital allocation to equity instruments only, while saving covers debt instruments only.

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Chapter 1 Section 1.1.1 explicitly separates the two: saving is the residual (earnings minus spending) typically held in short-term liquid instruments (cash, gold, short-term deposits), whereas investment is the commitment of those savings for a specific time period with an expectation of a higher return. The chapter states 'every investor is a saver but not vice versa.' Parking INR 40 cr in T-bills is saving-mode; the INR 60 cr in the Cat III long-short unit class is investment-mode. **The Trap:** Option A reflects the common loose usage that the chapter explicitly rejects. Option C reverses the 'every investor is a saver, not vice versa' logic. Option D fabricates an asset-class boundary that the chapter never draws — both equity and debt can sit on either side depending on horizon and intent. **Cross-Exam Context:** XXI-B (Portfolio Manager) and X-A (IA L1) test the same saving-vs-investment distinction for retail suitability. XIX-B (Cat III Distributor) frames it from the seller's side. XIX-E (this exam) frames it from the fund-desk perspective — why an HNI's T-bill sleeve is NOT the Cat III fund's mandate. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** When a Cat III open-ended fund onboards a family-office ticket, the IMA and PPM should clearly delineate what portion of the client's wealth is 'saving sleeve' (kept outside the fund in T-bills/liquid funds) versus 'investment sleeve' (the Cat III NAV unit). This distinction matters operationally because Cat III open-ended funds face daily redemption pressure — if an HNI confuses the two, they may redeem to fund short-term consumption, forcing the fund to unwind long-short pairs prematurely.
